lines.text: I'd like to call this meeting to order. Welcome here, everyone. And at this time, I would like to, uh, give the opening to Councillor Michael Zwaagstra, Deputy Mayor.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. It's been nearly 6 months since Hamas carried out its deadly October 7th terrorist attacks against Israel. On that day, more than 1,200 Israelis were brutally murdered and And approximately 240 were taken hostage by Hamas terrorists. In response, Israel declared war on Hamas and declared a— and launched a series of military strikes on the Gaza Strip. While Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau initially expressed solidarity with Israel, deep divisions in the Liberal caucus have caused his government to equivocate on that support. Last month, the NDP used its Opposition Day in the House of Commons to introduce a motion Recognizing a Palestinian state. At the last minute, the Liberals and NDP agreed on a series of amendments that watered down the original motion enough so that all but a handful of Liberal MPs could support it. The fact that the House of Commons would spend an entire day debating a motion that rewards an explicitly genocidal government for carrying out a series of brutal terrorist attacks is a sign of how muddled our country's foreign affairs policy has become. Now more than ever, we need clear thinking on this issue. Fortunately, retired philosopher and Steinbach resident Dr. Hendrik van der Bruggen has a new book out that is a must-read for anyone who wants to think critically about this topic. In untangling popular anti-Israel arguments, Dr. van der Bruggen dispels many of the most common myths and false assumptions about the Israel-Hamas conflict. For example, Israel's critics frequently claim that Israel is engaging in genocide against the Palestinians. However, Dr. Van den Bruggen reminds his readers that it was Hamas that started this war. If Hamas really cared about the Palestinian people, they would never have intentionally slaughtered 1,200 Israeli civilians on October 7th, something they knew would provoke a severe military response from Israel. Dr. Van der Bruggen also argues that intent matters in military conflicts. While Hamas intentionally targeted civilians on October 7th and uses women and children as human shields to maximize civilian casualties, Israel tries to avoid hitting civilian targets and warns Palestinian civilians to evacuate before engaging in a bombing campaign. Civilian casualties are always tragic, but there's a clear distinction between how Hamas and Israel conduct themselves in this matter. Another common claim is that Israel's response to Hamas has not been proportional. Critics regularly point to the lopsided casualty statistics and argue that since far more Palestinians than Israelis have been killed in the last 6 months, Israel is acting unjustly in its response. However, Dr. van der Bruggen points out that no other country has actually been held to this type of standard. The notion that since Hamas terrorists killed approximately 1,200 Israelis on October 7th, Israel must make sure it kills exactly 1,200 Palestinians in response is ridiculous. Under this reasoning, Israel should target a border village and rape the same number of women that Hamas terrorists raped, murder the same number of babies targeted by Hamas, and burn an equivalent number of Palestinian families alive in their own homes. Obviously ridiculous. Israel is at war with Hamas because it is seeking to eliminate that terrorist group's ability to carry out further terrorist attacks. Not only is that a worthwhile goal, but it is also the only acceptable outcome from this conflict. It is awful that Hamas is choosing to extend this conflict by refusing to surrender and to release their hostages, but that is the fault of Hamas, not Israel. Anyone interested in clear thinking about the Israel-Hamas conflict should get a copy of Dr. Van der Bruggen's book. There is far too much muddled reasoning about this issue in Canada today. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk
lines.title: Senior Manager, Finance
lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor, members of council. I am pleased to be presenting the city's 2024 financial plan to highlight some of the main items that are planned for the year. The annual budget cycle is almost a continuous process. For the 2024 budget year, it started early in 2023. Throughout the process, input is provided by staff, management, and council. The financial plan being presented today is based on the recommendations of council provided at their final review in November. Some of the highlights for 2024 include a municipal mill rate of 14.4 mills, which is an increase of just over 5% from 2023. Utility rates will increase by an average of 4%, while residential garbage collection rates will increase by 2.6%. Fees for permits are up 5%, and land use application fees will increase by 2.5%. The overall capital program for 2024 is budgeted at $62.7 million. Some of the larger budgeted projects include the completion of the event centre, the Loewen PTH 12 intersection renewal, Lift Station Number 2 upgrade, as well as the Hanover Street reconstruction. Overall, projected revenues for 2024 are just under $38.5 million. Similar to other years, property taxes are the city's largest source of revenue, accounting for roughly half of the overall revenue amount. For 2024, there was a property value growth of 4.4%. Commercial properties make up about 25% of the total property values in the city, and with the provincial portioning system, a lower portion of residential property values are subject to property tax than commercial property values. As I mentioned earlier, the property tax rate of 14.4 mills is up about 5% from 2023. Just note on the slides that were in your package, I think the property tax rate on that first bullet point says 14.1. That was an error. It should be 14.4. Thank you. Roughly half of the municipal revenues are from property taxes. $19.8 million is to be raised by property taxes in 2024, with $18.7 million of this via mill rate. The city is also required to collect the education and school taxes on behalf of the province and Hanover School Division. As in previous years, this is projected to make up roughly half of the total tax revenue collected by the city. The average market value for a dwelling in Steinbach is roughly $225,000. Based on this and the budgeted mill rate, the average city property tax bill works out to just over $120 a month. In addition to regular property taxes, supplementary Supplementary property taxes are levied on new construction or where there was an addition or improvement to increase the value of the property. This is expected to provide an additional $675,000 in 2024. Federal and provincial operating grants have also been a consistent source of revenue for the city. The provincial per capita tax sharing grant is expected to provide $4.6 million in 2024, while the federal gas tax grant will provide just over $890,000. One of the main non-tax revenues for the city is from user fees. These are fees paid by those who benefit from the service provided. Some services compete with the open market, but a number of the rates may be subsidized for programs to be accessible. Development in Steinbach stayed strong in 2023 with over $200 million in total permit values. This activity is expected to continue into 2024 and beyond. Now we will look at some of the programs that are funded by these revenues. Overall, the expenses are equal to the projected revenues at just under $38.5 million. Some 2024 programs include waste reduction and recycling at just over $1 million. Support for the Jake Epp Public Library at $453,000, the beautification program $267,000, and various other programs as listed. Every year the city provides grants for various organizations throughout the city. In 2024, these grants total just over $1 million with the recipients as listed. One of the largest city expenses is that of our employees. The total labor cost, including benefits, for 2024 is budgeted at $11.2 million, or roughly a third of the city's operating budget. Of this total, the aquatic center makes up about 18% of the total labor hours The largest of any city department. Protective services includes 18 RCMP officers, 46 firefighters and 8 trucks, as well as a community services officer to enforce city bylaws. The total cost of these services is budgeted at $5.1 million for the upcoming year. The city currently has over 144 kilometers of road surface. The maintenance for this infrastructure can depend fairly significantly on the weather in any given year, and for 2024 is expected to cost $2.9 million. Solid waste services. We provide both curbside and on-demand pickup services to both residential and commercial properties. The cost of providing these services is expected to reach $3.2 million for the upcoming year, which is funded by user fees. Our primary recreation facilities include the aquatic centre, arena, A.D. Penner Park, curling rink, and soccer park, as well as various green space and parks around the city. The expected cost of operating and maintaining these facilities is budgeted at $4.8 million for 2024. Both the number of customers serviced by the water and wastewater utility and the length of the underground infrastructure network continue to grow. The expected cost to maintain this infrastructure and provide the utility services is expected to be $4.5 million in 2024. In addition to the typical operating expenses that the city regularly incurs, larger projects also require significant funding. Some of this comes from reserve funds that have been saved in previous years, while While other projects will require debt funding. Some of the main projects for the upcoming year include equipment replacement, the event centre construction, and PTH 12 Loewen intersection. The total capital program for the year is expected to be just under $63 million. The city will periodically issue debt in order to add or renew various infrastructure or facilities Each loan will fund a specific project. In 2024, 2 projects have a debt component: the event centre construction and the Loewen Boulevard PTH 12 intersection. This is expected to create $16 million of new debt, while $1.5 million of previously issued debt will be paid off. The city continues to use a 5-year amortization term for all of its debt, allowing us to borrow at lower interest rates than than if a longer term was used. Our average interest rate for 2024 is just under 4.2%, while the debt balance at the end of the year is expected to be $19.5 million. Payments that are required for previously issued debt will total $1.7 million in 2024. Of this amount, $209,000 is interest. Funding for these debt payments is raised through property taxation, and for 2024, 1.27 mills will be required to raise the necessary funds. This equates to just under 9% of the total city tax rate. And finally, a longer-term overview of some of the expected requirements in future years. The 2024 program is currently budgeted at $62.7 million, which includes infrastructure renewal, the completion of the event center, and equipment replacement. Beyond that, programs of $20.1 million, $5 million, and $16.1 million are currently estimated for the following 3 years. That concludes the presentation of the 2024 financial plan. Thank you, members of council. If there are any questions, I can answer them now.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Well, every year we go through the budget process and that involves a lot of discussion This is a budget that has been developed through a lot of discussions and hard work by our staff. And I will say that in the years that I've been on council, I think this was our toughest budget. And the reason why it's so difficult is because we've been dealing with inflation, particularly in regards to construction costs. And I know that the city, we had released some information back in the fall giving some examples of projects where the amounts that it cost for some of our underground Renewal, it was just coming in well above the— our projected costs. This is not unique to us. We're seeing this across the country. I think pretty much every municipality you're seeing some form of increase. And as a council, we're not willing to sacrifice the quality of the services that people get. We're not willing to sacrifice in regards to our infrastructure program. And we are obviously moving ahead with the projects that we have. So what this leads us to is that if there is an increase of 5.1%, it increases to $14.4 mils. And again, that increase is mainly because of the increased— is mainly caused by inflation. And so we have a lot of projects that are happening this year in regards to infrastructure renewal. As was mentioned, the lift station, the upgrades along Hanover Street, the Highway 12 and Loewen Boulevard intersection, which we're doing in partnership with the province. And then of course our events centre is moving ahead, and obviously the cost in that has been quite significant. Thank you. That's significant. Interest rates are also higher on our loans, and so 4.18% average is still good when you look over the long term historically, but it's not the 2% that we've been used to getting for quite some time. And so when you're paying more interest on our debt, that also has an impact on our bottom line. And I should note that we are still sticking to our 5-year debt policy. Every single project that we're doing will be paid off in 5 years, including the event centre. I don't know of any municipality anywhere in the country that is building an event centre like what we have that will be debt-free in 5 years. That is something that I think we can be very proud of. It's been very difficult in terms of finding the money to make it work, but we've had good support from the private sector and from other levels of government, and we've been able to find the money to, to make that work. One of the advantages of our 5-year debt is that we're paying less interest, because if you do it over 20 years, you're obviously paying interest over a much longer period of time, and that significantly increases the cost. And so the total budget, just over $38 million. Again, we're sticking to our priorities. We, we haven't changed in that regard. We're still prioritizing our infrastructure. We'll still prioritize our recreation renewal. We're still funding the same number of RCMP officers, 18 officers. We're paying that. We're still making sure that our fire department is well funded and that they have good equipment and that we have an adequate number of firefighters. So we are continuing to provide the excellent services that, that people have become accustomed to. And the only way to be able to continue doing all that is to go with this budget, which does mean that this year that there is this increase. Thank you. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens

lines.text: Well, I don't know how much I can add to Councillor Zwaagstra, but maybe echo a few things. I think too this is a budget that is one of our toughest that we've had. One of the things that, uh, in the past we had a little bit of wiggle room, if that's the right word, is our supplementary property taxes where those were added We have been raising property taxes on new properties, and that would be found money. And in order to hold taxes in past years, we've also started to budget for those supplementary property taxes. So that has also now— we don't know what those supplementary taxes are till the end of the year, but as we go, we can't use too much of them, but we have been digging into those as well. We've also raised our user fees. For water, for sewer, for different events. So while those— some of those rates are subsidized, it also is pay for service. And so that's worked as well, as well as our provincial and federal granting. We've got commitments that that's going to go up, but we don't have those numbers necessarily either yet, so we can't budget for that. Okay. When we did the annexation 8 years ago, we added many kilometres of roads, 144 kilometres of roads today that our transportation services are taking care of. We're also adding water and sewer, and one of the key things this council has always done is focused on infrastructure renewal. And we have a lot fewer issues within our community with our infrastructure than many other communities have, and where we continue to do a lot of work. Our engineering department has been very good in providing us a lot of good information on how to year over year budget and rebuild and replace our infrastructure. One of the things we didn't want to do either with the— when we focused on the event center, we didn't want to cut back on our infrastructure renewal. That happened when the indoor pool was built. It was restricted for 5 years, and we also didn't want to do that. In order to keep up with our infrastructure renewal, we needed— we need to increase our tax base. As well, with our police and fire services, especially our police, when we were under 15,000 people in population, then the federal government paid 25% of our cost of Of RCMP officers. Now we are at 95% of cost. So that was a huge influx of dollars plus. So that has been part of it as well. And we always look to recreation services. Recreation services provide our quality of life in our community. We need more active transportation routes. We need more green space. We need more opportunities for people to get out and enjoy our community. And so it is We— I don't— in our term, I don't think we've ever raised more our budget by 5.1%. So I think this is a good budget. We have held back. We've taken some of our projects and we have spread them into upcoming years, our renewal projects. So I think— but I still think this is a good budget. I think it's one that we can stand behind because there will be a lot of work continue to be done in Steinbach, but also it is work that is essentially needed for long-term health.

We had the rec reserve, which really helped us. So a lot of good planning, and I'm excited about the budget. Thank you.

lines.title: Mayor

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Yeah, I stand by everything else that council has said in agreement, but it's important to remember that as municipally elected officials, we're dealing with a budget where there isn't a lot of discretionary spending. You know, I don't hear residents saying that they want dirtier water or their toilets not to flush. That they want the roads to fall apart, that they don't want the garbage collected, you know, police and fire services. These are essential items on our budget line that is not discretionary, and we can't really be— we can't move on that. Then when you go and you look at our budget and we're adding $16.5 million in this budget year to infrastructure renewal, which is incredibly important. The City of Steinbach, we talk about the growth of the city, but it's also important to remember that It's an older— it's an old city, and there is infrastructure that constantly is needing to be renewed, and we need to stay on top of that because without— with kicking the can down the road, you create bigger problems later and more expensive problems later, and then you're looking at where do you find the shortfall. And I think that's one thing that we on council here pride ourselves is sticking to the 5-year amortization, and we don't want to have to start deviating from that. So sometimes that will mean the hard decisions of temporary increases to then find the benefit later and continued through the life of the city. So this is a budget that it's a hard pill to swallow to have to look at an increase, but it is a necessary one in my opinion.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.text: Thank you. Well, council, it is hard to add to anything that has been said. Because I do agree with it as well. And you know what, we're all in the room. When we're giving up our days, we're giving up our weekends, and our staff are doing the same. And on top of that, the staff have to put up with us and our arguing backwards and forwards, right? And, but council, this is a good budget because we've all had input, we've all said what is important to us, That into our budget. And some things that have been important to us, we've had to pull out and put into next year's budget or the year after because it just can't all get done with one budget. When you look at a $62.7 million capital budget between borrowing, between reserves, between our general, general, income. That is really aggressive. That is very progressive. We are a very progressive council. We're getting— there's getting— we're getting a lot of work done and there's a lot of development in our community because I believe we are proactive, because we do make sure our roads are in good shape. We make sure that there is lots to build on and we make sure that we are negotiating with the governments that are there above us in order to get grants so that we can, we can make this happen for our community, even though in areas where it's not our jurisdiction. But we work and advocate in healthcare so that we can have good healthcare for our, for our people. So, because we know that that will just grow our community and bring more people to it. It's, it's very exciting to see a budget like this. This, I would agree with Councillor Siemens. I don't think we've— I can't remember a time that we've actually intentionally grew the budget, like we just— that we had an increase of 5%. But given the fact with that, what we're facing with inflation, the fact that we— what we're facing with the renewal that has to happen, I think that, It's appropriate for this time. And I'm looking forward to this budget. I'm looking forward to these projects getting finished. And council, I just want to thank— I want to thank staff and I want to thank council for what you've done. This budget doesn't just happen. It's because there's many people that are working on this budget and many people are Putting in their ideas and their desires and their wants and what they love about our community. And sometimes we have to put things on hold too. But I think, I think this is a balanced budget, and I think that this budget will, will suit us well in 2024. Thank you. lines.label: Bill Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I totally agree with this. It's a good plan because the road isn't running right through Back to the number 12 highway, so a turning circle makes sense. And this is a good subdivision. I think this will work out well.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further, council? Anything in closing?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: No, thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Council, yes, sometimes as these developments go forward, there are changes that are needed. They come back to us and we make those changes. In this case, the biggest changes that are happening here, as was stated, was a turnaround and the widening of a road. So I think that, that, that looks good. There's been no, no objections. So call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. Okay, thank you. We move on to 7A. This is our delegation. We're a little bit late. It's 8:05. But it's Staff Sergeant Guy Landerville will be coming and presenting to us the annual update and his— the policing priorities. Good evening. How are you today? We are fine, or I am fine. How, how are you?

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Good, thank you. Okay, so I'm just going to present some stats. To everyone here. I have 2 of them. I have the usual, the 4th quarter ones for—

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: That is really not really any different than the year end. If I could start with the year end, I think the ones that's presently that you have in front of you now. And just talk a little bit about what we've been facing over the last year. To begin with, traffic accidents are on the rise, or they have gone up from '22 to '23. Not significantly, I might add, but normally what we're seeing, if, if the speeding on number 2 has increased, and normally we'll see if the traffic offenses are on the rise, then normally accidents will go the other way. Okay. Right now, they tend— the traffic offenses as a whole are down. We're trying to rectify that with our—

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: We have the newly created traffic position, not new as far as time, but I have a new officer that's dedicated to that position right now, and so far is doing tremendous work.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: And we're trying to improve on that. We're trying to get—

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: We're trying to do a little bit more traffic-oriented work. Okay. And we can, uh, we can elaborate on that if you wish in a little bit.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: And, uh, but for now, it's, it's a work in progress, and, uh, we hope to be able to do more on the traffic side than we have in the past. Our impaired numbers are up. The provincial statutes are down, but that number 4 is mostly due to a lot of leftover COVID investigation that are now starting to, to go by the wayside. So that's why that number's on the negative side. Other criminal code up a little bit, 36. Frauds are up as well. Drug enforcement was up a little bit. The good, good news is crime against persons, the sexual assaults are down, and the assaults are up, but only maybe by 11, which is Same as harassment and threats, which is not really that significant over the course of the year. What gets significant is— let me see here— 11 is not bad at 28. That's getting a little bit higher than it was. The theft overs, robberies are at 0, so that there's no increase. That's, that's really good news. Theft of vehicles is actually down, so that's excellent news. The break-and-enters is what is significant, and mischief as well. Approaches to these type of crimes in the past was, you know, we'll arrest the culprits, put them in jail, and that'll take care of the problem. What we're seeing now is a lot of revolving door jail policies where a lot of the culprits are not Are not really dealt with as far as being incarcerated for any amount of time, and it causes us further problems when they're just released as quickly as they're put in.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: And we have recent examples of that. Most of what we're seeing are the break-and-enters, maybe not the mischief, but most of what we're seeing with break-and-enters and some of the thefts are addiction-driven. So the people that are committing them are, for the most part, the same people. They're doing the same ones over and over again. Thank you. They're addicted to methamphetamine and other substances, and in order to, to continue taking meth and, and, and continue with that lifestyle, they, they need money.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: For the most part, these people live— they're very poor and have to continue stealing in order to get money and buy meth and feed their addiction.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: So traditional approaches right now are not really working as far as arrest, put in jail, and hope that the justice system will take care of these people. This is why Heidi is with me today from Headway, and she'll make it—

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Just give you guys a little bit of an approach, or she'll talk a little bit about what they do. And in a nutshell, we're trying to, to help these people with their addictions and get them all the resources and the help that they need. In order for them to come clean and to be, you know, members of society that can, that can hopefully, you know, get some employment and work and, and, and stop doing what they're doing is what we're trying to do. So we've had some success with it, and Heidi can talk to you a little bit about that a little bit later, a little more in detail. Okay. But there are success stories, and again, it's difficult to measure because it's saying, well, you know, if, if the B&Es are up 15%, And we've helped 4 people, you know, does that take care of the 15%? So it's hard to actually put numbers to it. What the best I can do is, is, is address the, the success stories that we have. And right now it's pretty much, you know, we're, we're not gonna put all our eggs in the same basket, but we're, you know, if we have a dozen, we'll probably put 10 in that Headway basket right now. Because like I said, traditional, traditional ways of doing things in the old days is, is basically not working. And like I said before, to repeat myself, it's the same people doing the same crimes over for the same reason. You know, they're addicted, they want more methamphetamine or other drugs that they're taking, they don't have the means to support their addiction, so they go and commit crime.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much for your presentation. And before Heidi comes on, I'm just wondering if I could just ask you one question about the speeding, because the speeding did jump drastically from 2022 to 2023. Yes. Now, would you, would you relate that exactly to the, the dedicated traffic officer that we had? Yes. Okay.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: And, and I will guarantee you that when you see the 2024 in comparison next year, that number will be even higher.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: So it's going to get even better. He was— the member was doing a good job, and, and I, and I praise him for that. And the member that I have now will do a great job.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: So just from, from what I'm seeing right now, it's an increase, and, uh, and it's, and it's overdue because I see a lot of it myself if I'm driving my kids to school in the morning or going home. And like we were talking before, with stop signs, for example, and And the speeding that we see, the, the racing, which has calmed down quite a bit, but we continuously see that. And with that comes visibility as far as people wanting to see us as well. So if you put that all together, I think traffic is important. One member is great. I think more is better. So I'm not trying to tell you how to do your job. I'm just trying to tell you That I think it's very important because it's, it's not only safer, but it takes care of the visibility aspect as well, and it, and it takes care of the community safety. It's like I said, it's, it's a safety issue. And, uh, knock on wood, so far we haven't had anything that serious as far as traffic collisions are concerned. But the way I'm seeing it myself, um, I think it could get It could get bad based on, you know, we're saying the, the roads are now 100 and how many kilometers? 144. 144 compared to what they used to be. So you're playing, you're playing a little bit of a game right now and just saying, I think one officer will do the job. I'm sure he will, but I think we have to be cautious. We have to be, we have to take this seriously and say, you know what, now everything's increasing. We've got New subdivisions coming in, new people moving in. We got a big event centre getting built. More traffic, more traffic.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: We do have the— we still have the traffic division that's from the province that works out of the detachment.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Right, right.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Do you have— is there— do they also do tours in our city? Like, do they spend time in our city?

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Yes, yes, they do. That's not their main focus right now. It's still the, the ring road in and around Winnipeg, but it is. I will send them requests and ask if they do specific hotspots that are brought up by the public, and they do. And I report back to the different RMs or municipalities that have suggested or requested those patrols. So yes, yes, they do them. And yeah, so their numbers of officers as well is getting— is increasing, which is nice to see.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Well, I want to give your team a pat on the back, especially the traffic officer, because being a business on Main Street, I've seen a huge reduction in the racing and the revving of cars and just the noise that Main Street has brought, that those Hot rods or tuners or whatever, what the guys that were coming to race, whoever they were, and the noise they were making, I've seen a vast reduction in that. And so if we can— and nothing's perfect, but if we can continue to work on that, I think, I think now it's— it might even have moved to other areas of our community, but we've got great people in our community and they alert us of that. And when we talk to you I know you've always had a sympathetic ear and you've always put someone on those areas and we're thankful for what you do. And, but before Heidi comes, are there any questions for— go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Through you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Welcome back. This is your second time at council here, so.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Yes, it is, yes.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: A familiar face now. Do you have your— I think there's 18 officers and— Do you have your full complement of officers that you can use?

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: For the most part. I'm down one, as we call, a hard vacancy, and right now I'm working with staffing to fill that. We have other, other vacancies referred to as soft vacancies, so maternity leave, paternity leave, and different off-duty sickness that is basically out of our control. But for the, for the most part, we're getting, we're getting close. Now it's difficult to, to predict maternity and paternity leaves. It's— I only have presently one, and— but they, as you know, they can change, and they're not replaced, by the way. So, and neither is any long-term sickness or short-term sickness as well. That can be— that can get a little tricky.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Do we— go ahead, one more. The GIS unit, that's still working? Is there one or 2 constables in there?

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: One corporal and one constable. I've had to draw on their, on their, on that unit to help out during shortages because of different vacancies, but for the most part they've been busy. We've, we've done quite a few search warrants that I've participated in as well and taken down last time a few, few pounds of methamphetamine along with a couple of traffickers. So they're very effective. A lot of information that led to a lot of search warrants as well. So they are doing their work, and it's not— the numbers are not going up because they're not there or they're not doing their work. The work is getting done. But as you must, you must understand that this drug, the methamphetamine drug, is extremely addictive and extremely cheap so that a lot more people can partake compared to cocaine in the '70s. which was a rich man's drug, and today with the methamphetamine, you can— $10 or $15 and you can be high for 3 days. So it's extra— it's, uh, and there's lots of it in— there's lots of it here. Yeah.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. Anything further? Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Again, thank you for the work that you and your men and women do every day here in Steinbach. Appreciate it. Thank you. I want to make a comment about the dedicated I have a question for the traffic personnel that we have here in the city. As you're probably aware, more than 20 years ago, I advocated for a special dedicated policeman to do just traffic in Steinbach, and I was excited when council passed that resolution to hire that extra man, I think a year and a half or 2 years ago. So that was good. And my reasoning at that time was to— if we have extra patrols, Extra enforcement, extra warnings, extra visibility, that it would cause less stress on paramedics, less stress on the police, less stress on hospitals, less physical damage to people, and of course more safety to the residents of this community. And so when I saw the accident statistic That it had gone up. I was— and I'm not blaming anybody on— I was kind of surprised to see that, that with the enforcement that we've had and that you've told us here today, that the accidents have gone up. And so I don't know what the rationale would be, what the reasoning would be behind it. It just happened. Great. Stuff does happen, so I say that. But— and when you're talking for about a second person on traffic. My views all the time, or my goal for us for a dedicated traffic person, was that MPI would eventually pay for that person. So hopefully we can get the accidents down and get MPI to sponsor that second person.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Yes, that's, that's an excellent, excellent point.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: And when you talk about the revolving door, the rotating door, I fully agree with you. And I think lately we had that guy from a Canada-wide warrant was released, and the next thing we find out, he commits a murder. So, but that is the legislation that you have to work under. So I appreciate the work you do.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Well, thank you. We're trying— I'm always trying to work or think outside the box, come up with some solutions. That's why Heidi and, and Brenda, I'm going to be working closely with them Because I think it's effective. It's— we have success stories. We can get you some stats as well, and we can look at that. And but overall, I think it's a great initiative, and I think it'll— it speaks for itself.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, you had a question, Councillor?

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Yeah, thank you, Mr. Mayor, and I thank you for the work you're doing. And in terms of the dedicated traffic officer, obviously, as you've reported, it's making a difference. And we're certainly getting far fewer complaints about racing on Main Street. Are you finding that, that as the enforcement has been largely successful in Main Street, that there are other areas where have become hotspots? And if you don't want to name the particular areas, that's fine because you don't want to give away your strategy. But are you finding that some of that is shifting to other areas, or is it fairly random in terms of where that problem happens? And other— it happens in other parts of the city?

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Yeah, I think it's— it is random. Before it was a dedicated area, and I think we've stomped that one into the ground pretty good. And we haven't really seen any other areas. Like I said, it's here and there we get the odd call, but it's not like saying, okay, we can't go in front of your shop anymore, so we're going to go somewhere else. So we haven't seen that. Not to say that it won't happen, but right now we haven't seen anything like that.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, good.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Anything further, council? Thank you very much, Guy. Thank you for what you do in our community, and thank you for your openness, and you're willing to work together in the RCMP advisory committee to make Steinbach a safer community.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Thank you, thank you very much.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: We— you were a pleasure to work with, and we're thankful that we have you.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Thank you, thank you so much.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you. You wanted to talk about the priorities as well, or We, you, we can go over that, then when you're completely done with Heidi and that, then, okay, then we will, um, make a resolution to approve them. But okay, we can totally go over them. Let's go over them.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Oh, okay, good. So yeah, as on my annual performance plan, I've got basically the 5 priority objectives that we're working on. The first one is obviously communication, talking about visibility of the police. Crime reduction, number 2, organized crime. That's where my GIS guys kick in. We're also trying to reduce crime, property crimes, vandalism, and that's— Heidi will talk a little bit more about that. And the crime reduction for traffic as well, we've spoken about that. And the last one is respectful workplace, so I think that just goes without saying. I think everywhere is Pretty much the same. So we have a small strategy in-house for things like that. So great.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Well, thank you very much.

lines.speaker: Guy Landreville
lines.title: RCMP Staff Sergeant
lines.label: Guy Landreville (RCMP Staff Sergeant, RCMP Steinbach Detachment)
lines.text: Thank you. I'll bring Heidi up here to talk a little bit about her workshop and what she does.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Hello. Hello. Welcome here.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Thank you. So yeah, my name is Heidi Harder Falk. I'm the youth coordinator with Headway, and it was mentioned to me I need to state my address as well.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Oh yeah, for just for the minutes.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Yeah, for records for sure. So, so Headway business address is at the Steinbach RCMP detachment, and so that's 100 PTH 12 North in Steinbach.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Yeah, so I think probably For the most part, you're familiar with Headway from Brenda Brown. She's our adult coordinator. It's my first time as youth coordinator coming before all of you, so it's great to meet you all and to be here. So yeah, I've been the youth coordinator with Headway for a little over a year now, and so with that, I work with the youth ages around 12 to 19. Okay. And then Brenda with our Adult Restart Program for justice-involved adults. That's anyone ages 18 and up. So yeah, on the—

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: For both of our programs, we do community mobilization wraparound support type work.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so as part of that, we partner with the RCMP, with probation services, shared health, Okay. So we work with the 3 main partners, which includes the Addictions Foundation, Southern Health, which includes community mental health, and then there's also the Hanover School Division and CFS. And so, so we have a lot of great partnerships with them, but then we'll also work with a number of other organizations in the community who provide different supports and services in, in any ways that our clients might benefit from.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: So we really appreciate working with them as well.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so yeah, I'll mostly just be focusing on the crime prevention side of things for now because yeah, I mean, for Brenda's adult program, of course, all of those individuals are justice involved, and my youth clients right now, all of them are as well, and so there's definitely high justice involvement for all of them.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so yeah, what we, what we work with there is again just that community mobilization wraparound support piece where, like the Staff Sergeant mentioned, there are so many situations where crime is coming out of substance use issues or mental health issues or just different things going on.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so to be able to look at all of those issues in an individual's life and, and to be able to work on building support teams that will wrap around the individual. And in the case of the youth program, their, their caregivers as well, um, is, is just really instrumental in being able to make sure they're supported and held accountable. And then that those teams meet on a monthly basis as well for that ongoing work.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And, and so yeah, as far as, as far as justice system involvement goes, what we see on the youth side is that after becoming involved with Headway, we're seeing around or above a 90% reduction in, in youth involvement with the justice system. And that could be charges, it could be mental health calls or wellness checks, people going missing. It can be a variety of things in that way.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And on the adult side, also again around the 90% or above mark, Okay.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Reduced involvement with the RCMP since becoming involved with the Restart Program. And, and then with that too, there's high percentages of them are getting connected with therapy, getting connected with substance use supports, community mental health. A number of those different supports are put into place there.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: So those are some of the Yeah, some of the justice system crime pieces that we're working with, and yeah, again, just really great results that we're seeing there, and just other areas that we're able to work in the community to do some of those more preventative pieces as well.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Whether yeah, I mean, so council is familiar, I understand, with the community.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Safety and well-being initiative that's moving through.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: There's— I, as the youth coordinator, I'm also part of the Steinbach Alternative Justice Committee. And there are just different parent supports and groups that we've been able to run in the community as well. And so a lot more of those preventative or early intervention type pieces as well that we're really working to bring more into the community as well. So, uh, yeah, that is kind of what, uh, the work that we do on that side. And just a, a short story on kind of the impact from our adult side. Um, we had a, a, a female client some time ago who grew up in the foster care system, um, and primarily involved Okay.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: With the justice system through assaults and a lot of just very aggressive behaviors.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so since becoming involved with Restart, she was able to access help just navigating through the court system, the legal process, and also getting connected to therapy, getting connected to addictions assessments and, and supports, and was able to secure employment.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: So with that as well, there has been no reoffending, and, and yeah, just one of those examples whereby addressing the reasons behind her behavior, we've been able to support in just doing a complete 180 there.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And, and yeah, her being able to again secure work, have a place to live, have formal and informal supports, be building community, and so You just see the thriving there.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: And so, yeah, that's it for what I have to share for today. Thank you so much for listening.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Well, thank you very, very much, Heidi, for coming out and giving us a snapshot of what you do and how closely you work with the RCMP. And I have heard these stories before, but they're always good to hear, the good stories that come out of Headway. And what you do. And I think I remember the first year there was 19 youth that went through the program. Out of the 19, 17 stopped having interaction with the RCMP altogether. Right. And the last 2, I believe they, due to family dynamics or something, they moved away, but they were also placed in other care. Care of other people at the time. So I don't know what happened to those last 2, but when I look at those numbers, you know, that 17 of the— so basically 17 of the 17 that stayed stopped having interaction with the police. You know, that's a very positive thing because that starts positive things in their life. And that's what Headway does. And you work together with Guy and his team. And that's— I mean, that's a great resource to have. And you were a big part of our community wellness and safety initiative. I do believe that. I think that's a big part of it. Councillor, are there any questions for Heidi? Okay. You've done a great presentation because there's no questions. Perfect. We know that you answered everything right from the start. So thank you very much for coming out, and we hope to see To see you again. Mm-hmm, yeah. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Heidi Harder-Falk
lines.title: Headway Youth Coordinator
lines.label: Heidi Harder-Falk (Headway Youth Coordinator, Headway Program)
lines.text: Oh, I'm sure you will. Thank you again.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Okay, council, there is one item that we did go through over with Staff Sergeant Guy Landerville on page 102. He has put forward the priorities and objectives that he is looking for to work on in our community. Number 1 being communication, the visibility of the police, the crime reduction retaining to or pertaining to organized crime, crime reduction pertaining to property crimes, B&Es, and vandalism, crime reduction as pertaining to traffic, and also to have a workplace, a respectful workplace environment for his members. Council, if you can agree with these, Uh, we would like to, by resolution, approve the priorities for 2024. Councillor Zwaagstra.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I'll make the motion to approve these priorities for the upcoming year.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Seconded by Councillor Penner. Go ahead, Councillor.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Deputy Mayor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Deputy Mayor)
lines.text: Uh, thank you, Mr. Mayor. Certainly appreciate the work of our, uh, RCMP staff sergeant and the other RCMP members, as well as the organizations such as Headway that, uh, partner with them in their efforts. These priorities are a good reflection of what we want to see out of police in our community. We want them to be visible. We want to focus on crime reduction and organized crime. That's what our GIS unit focuses on, doing the long-term investigations of some of the, some of the bigger crime issues, property crimes, break-and-enters and such, reducing that, focusing on that. That is important too. And of course, we talk a lot about traffic because we have a lot of traffic in our city, and we've in the past had significant issues with, in particular, racing on Main Street, which we are definitely addressing with the dedicated officer there. We want that priority to continue, and we want the message to be out loud and clear that if you're thinking of racing in Steinbach, particularly on our Main Street, don't, don't come to Steinbach to race because you will get ticketed, you will have your vehicle impounded. And we have certainly told our staff sergeant at our RCMP advisory meetings, and as Council as a whole, show no mercy, give them every ticket you possibly can, take their vehicles away. And so we certainly do support these, these priorities and keep up the good work.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much. Anything further?

lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor) [medium]
lines.text: Nothing further to add.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Anything closing? Yeah, council, just to summarize, I will say I too also agree. I think these, these fit with our priorities in our community as well. Well, and these are things we want to see happen in our community. Of course, crime reduction— who doesn't want to see crime reducing? And I do believe we've got the right people on the job for that, and they're working hard for us. Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? Carried. Thank you very much. Okay, council, we will move on to 8A. This is reports and recommendations from our city manager. This is referring to landfill loader purchase. It starts on page 103. And Mr. Warkentin, could you please introduce this file?

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This item is a package of information for council to be able to consider the purchase of a new Thank you. This is a John Deere 624 loader from Brandt Tractor Ltd. The previous loader that was in use by the city was damaged and written off by our insurer earlier this year. The city did receive a payout of funds under the insurance claim that will be used to fund this new loader, and the loader was publicly sourced through The city's purchasing group, Canoe Service through AMM, with a price of $358,000 plus applicable taxes. And as this amount of the bid exceeds the limit of the city manager to approve financial purchases, this must be approved by council through resolution recommending is for council to approve this purchase from Brandt Tractor for the 624 John Deere loader.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Warkentin. Council, how would you like to proceed? Councillor Hiebert?

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: Motion to approve.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Second by Councillor Hiebert. Go ahead.

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jake Hiebert (Councillor)
lines.text: It's— thank you, Mr. Mayor. It's unfortunate that we have to replace the equipment at the landfill site, As indicated, it's a 624 John Deere loader. Our city has— manager's done due diligence, public sourced, and quotes have been received, and the lowest price is indicated here. And if we want the landfill to continue working, we need equipment. So thank you, and for the work that the administration has done to get the lowest price.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, Councillor Hiebert?

lines.speaker: Bill Hiebert

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Anything further, council? Call for the question. All those in favour? That is carried. We've got 9A, administration, accounts payable, back of the book. We've all had a chance to review. Looking for a motion to approve. Councillor Penner. Seconded by Councillor Stevens. Any comments?

lines.text: Call for the question. All those in favor? Opposed? That is carried. We have 9C. This is a street renaming bylaw 2242. This is referring to Clearspring Drive to Blind Creek Boulevard. lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. This particular roadway is located just north of the Clearspring Mall in Steinbach. Recommendation is for this bylaw to be given third reading.
